1| #!/usr/bin/env bash
2| # orient — Sexton's wake-up brief for the fleet.
3| #
4| # Runs on the workstation; reaches out to z620 and Vultr over ssh with
5| # read-only probes (stock commands, invoked plainly — if you need a modified
6| # behavior, fork it under a new name, never shadow the real tool).
7| #
8| # Batons are data sources on disk. Found by value with grep; read by key with
9| # jq/flatten. Remote batons are fetched into a temp dir that dies with the
10| # script — nothing persists except the report.
11| #
12| # Reports in orients/ are historical and fungible: any session may rewrite
13| # this script's structure, so only orients/latest.txt is trustworthy, and only
14| # because you can read this file and see exactly where every number came from.
15| # If you want data over time, build a recorder; do not scrape old reports.
16| #
17| # Edit this script freely. Nothing is special because it is old.
18| 
19| set -uo pipefail
20| cd "$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")"
21| 
22| STAMP=$(date -u '+%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ')
23| mkdir -p orients
24| exec > >(tee "orients/orient-$STAMP.txt")
25| ln -sfn "orient-$STAMP.txt" orients/latest.txt
26| printf 'report: orients/orient-%s.txt\n' "$STAMP" >&2
27| 
28| section() { printf '\n## %s\n' "$1"; }
29| sub()     { printf '\n### %s\n' "$1"; }
30| 
31| SSH_OPTS=(-o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=8 -o ServerAliveInterval=5 -o ServerAliveCountMax=2)
32| Z620=studi@10.0.0.10
33| VULTR=vultr
34| 
35| # ---------------------------------------------------------------- batons ----
36| # Data sources. Local paths are literal; remote ones are fetched once into a
37| # temp dir so every later query is a local jq call. Edit when the fleet moves.
38| TMPD=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMPD"' EXIT
39| 
40| fetch_baton() { # name host path
41|   ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$2" "cat $3" >"$TMPD/$1.json" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "$TMPD/$1.json"
42| }
43| fetch_baton clawd          "$Z620"  /home/hopper/clawd/baton.json
44| fetch_baton neoclaw        "$Z620"  /home/hopper/clawd/projects/neoclaw/baton.json
45| fetch_baton neoclaw_rails  "$Z620"  /home/hopper/clawd/projects/neoclaw_rails/baton.json
46| fetch_baton catalog        "$Z620"  /home/hopper/clawd/town/services/parallax-catalog/baton.json
47| fetch_baton vultr          "$VULTR" /root/baton.json
48| 
49| shopt -s nullglob
50| BATONS=(identity.json baton.json projects/*/project.json "$TMPD"/*.json)
51| [ -f ~/Coding_Projects/semantic-chunking/baton.json ] && BATONS+=(~/Coding_Projects/semantic-chunking/baton.json)
52| 
53| baton_name() { # file -> project/resident name
54|   jq -r '.identity.name // .resident.name // .name // empty' "$1" 2>/dev/null | head -n1
55| }
56| 
57| # One structural pass per baton: every "port"/"*_port" field becomes a claim.
58| # Claims are "port<TAB>name<TAB>hosthint" in $TMPD/claims. Host hint comes
59| # from the entry's own host field, else the baton's surface.host, else the
60| # machine the baton was fetched from; empty means "any host".
61| : >"$TMPD/claims"
62| claim_file() { # file srchost
63|   local f=$1 srchost=$2 n
64|   [ -f "$f" ] || return
65|   n=$(baton_name "$f"); n=${n:-$(basename "$f" .json)}
66|   jq -r --arg n "$n" --arg srchost "$srchost" '
67|     def asport: if type == "number" and . == floor and . > 0 and . < 65536 then .
68|                 elif type == "string" and test("^[0-9]+$") then tonumber
69|                 else empty end;
70|     . as $root
71|     | [ paths(scalars) as $p
72|         | select(($p[-1] | type) == "string")
73|         | select($p[-1] == "port" or ($p[-1] | endswith("_port")))
74|         | (getpath($p) | asport) as $port
75|         | { port: $port,
76|             who: (if ($p | length) >= 3 and $p[0] == "active_threads" then $p[1] else $n end),
77|             ip: ((try getpath($p[:-1] + ["host"])) // ($root.surface.host?) // ($root.host?) // $srchost) }
78|       ] | unique | .[] | "\(.port)\t\(.who)\t\(.ip)"' "$f" 2>/dev/null >>"$TMPD/claims"
79| }
80| claim_file identity.json workstation
81| for f in baton.json projects/*/project.json; do claim_file "$f" ""; done
82| [ -f ~/Coding_Projects/semantic-chunking/baton.json ] && claim_file ~/Coding_Projects/semantic-chunking/baton.json ""
83| for rb in clawd neoclaw neoclaw_rails catalog; do claim_file "$TMPD/$rb.json" 10.0.0.10; done
84| claim_file "$TMPD/vultr.json" 96.30.195.214
85| 
86| port_owner() { # port hostlabel -> claiming project (empty if none)
87|   awk -F'\t' -v p="$1" -v h="$2" '
88|     $1 == p && ($3 == "" || $3 == h \
89|       || (h == "z620"  && $3 == "10.0.0.10") \
90|       || (h == "vultr" && $3 == "96.30.195.214")) {print $2; exit}' "$TMPD/claims"
91| }
92| 
93| # ---------------------------------------------------------------- report ----
94| section "Sexton orient"
95| printf '%-16s %s\n' generated_utc: "$STAMP"
96| printf '%-16s %s\n' host: "$(hostname)"
97| printf '%-16s %s\n' user: "$(whoami)"
98| 
99| section "Read first"
100| printf '%s\n' \
101|   '- Expected: z620 healthy; .home DNS answers 10.0.0.10; catalog/valley HTTP 200; valley websocket via Caddy 400; theuncannyvalley.cc HTTPS 502 (dead proxy until catalog static hosting replaces it); absurdrabbit.net has no A record.' \
102|   '- WARN lines are the orientation delta. No WARNs = the world matches the inherited map.' \
103|   '- Every number below sits next to the command that produced it in this script. Trust latest.txt only; older reports describe an older script.'
104| 
105| sub "workspace git"
106| git status --short --branch 2>/dev/null || true
107| 
108| section "Batons (data sources on disk)"
109| for f in "${BATONS[@]}"; do
110|   [ -f "$f" ] || continue
111|   n=$(baton_name "$f"); n=${n:-$(basename "$f" .json)}
112|   printf '%-24s %s\n' "$n" "${f/#$TMPD\//remote:}"
113| done
114| for pair in clawd neoclaw neoclaw_rails catalog vultr; do
115|   [ -f "$TMPD/$pair.json" ] || printf 'WARN: remote baton missing: %s\n' "$pair"
116| done
117| 
118| section "Open ports (reality, annotated from batons)"
119| 
120| printf '%-13s %-7s %-5s %-5s %-18s %s\n' host port proto bind process project
121| 
122| emit_ports() { # host proto collapse_unknown < ss -lnH[p] lines
123|   # One row per port, with bind scope. collapse_unknown=yes folds rows no
124|   # baton claims into a single NOTE (the workstation's ephemeral game/Steam
125|   # UDP firehose is not orientation signal).
126|   local host=$1 proto=$2 collapse=$3 laddr port owner
127|   local unknown=0
128|   declare -A procof=() scope=()
129|   while read -r _ _ _ laddr _ rest; do
130|     port=${laddr##*:}
131|     [[ $port =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || continue
132|     if [ -z "${procof[$port]+x}" ]; then
133|       procof[$port]=$(sed -n 's/.*users:(("\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' <<<"$rest")
134|     fi
135|     case $laddr in
136|       127.* | *::1*) : ;;
137|       *) scope[$port]=lan ;;
138|     esac
139|   done
140|   for port in $(printf '%s\n' "${!procof[@]}" | grep . | sort -n); do
141|     owner=$(port_owner "$port" "$host")
142|     if [ "$collapse" = yes ] && [ -z "$owner" ]; then unknown=$((unknown+1)); continue; fi
143|     printf '%-13s %-7s %-5s %-5s %-18s %s\n' "$host" "$port" "$proto" "${scope[$port]:-lo}" "${procof[$port]:--}" "${owner:-unknown}"
144|   done
145|   [ "$unknown" -gt 0 ] && printf 'NOTE: %s has %d unclaimed %s listeners not shown (ephemeral desktop/game ports)\n' "$host" "$unknown" "$proto"
146| }
147| 
148| ( sudo -n ss -lntHp 2>/dev/null || ss -lntHp ) | emit_ports workstation tcp no
149| ( sudo -n ss -lnuHp 2>/dev/null || ss -lnuHp ) | emit_ports workstation udp yes
150| ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$Z620"  'sudo -n ss -lntHp' 2>/dev/null | emit_ports z620 tcp no
151| ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$Z620"  'sudo -n ss -lnuHp' 2>/dev/null | emit_ports z620 udp no
152| ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$VULTR" 'ss -lntHp' 2>/dev/null | emit_ports vultr tcp no
153| ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$VULTR" 'ss -lnuHp' 2>/dev/null | emit_ports vultr udp no
154| 
155| sub "firewall openings with no listener"
156| z620_listen=$( { ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$Z620" 'sudo -n ss -lntHn; sudo -n ss -lnuHn' 2>/dev/null; } | awk '{print $4}' | sed 's/.*://' | grep -E '^[0-9]+$' | sort -u )
157| ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$Z620" 'sudo -n ufw status' 2>/dev/null \
158|   | awk '/ALLOW|LIMIT/ {split($1,a,"/"); if (a[1] ~ /^[0-9]+$/) print a[1]}' | sort -u \
159|   | comm -23 - <(printf '%s\n' "$z620_listen") \
160|   | while read -r p; do printf 'WARN: z620:%s allowed by ufw but nothing listens\n' "$p"; done
161| vultr_listen=$( { ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$VULTR" 'ss -lntHn; ss -lnuHn' 2>/dev/null; } | awk '{print $4}' | sed 's/.*://' | grep -E '^[0-9]+$' | sort -u )
162| ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" "$VULTR" 'iptables -S' 2>/dev/null \
163|   | sed -n 's/.*--dport \([0-9]*\).* -j ACCEPT/\1/p' | sort -u \
164|   | comm -23 - <(printf '%s\n' "$vultr_listen") \
165|   | while read -r p; do printf 'WARN: vultr:%s accepted by iptables but nothing listens\n' "$p"; done
166| 
167| section "Names and reachability"
168| sub "DNS"
169| for name in catalog.home valley.home git.home tickets.home absurdrabbit.net theuncannyvalley.cc; do
170|   printf '%-24s %s\n' "$name:" "$(dig +time=3 +tries=1 "$name" A +short 2>/dev/null | paste -sd, -)"
171| done
172| for name in catalog.home valley.home git.home tickets.home; do
173|   printf '%-24s %s\n' "$name@z620:" "$(dig +time=3 +tries=1 @10.0.0.10 "$name" A +short 2>/dev/null | paste -sd, -)"
174| done
175| sub "HTTP"

177|   printf '%-34s %s\n' "$url" "$(curl -sS -o /dev/null --max-time 12 -w '%{http_code} from %{remote_ip} in %{time_total}s' "$url" 2>&1)"

1| # The Orient Baton
2| 
3| **Written:** 2026-09-17, the night of the caveman incident and the compaction autopsy.
4| **Authors:** Sexton, with Evans, in conversation.
5| **Status:** Concept complete. Implementation in progress by Evans (root `orient` executable, `orients/` snapshots, appeared 23:54 during the design conversation; unreviewed by Sexton, awaiting finalization together). If you are a future session reading this before the system is ratified: your job is to hold the idea, not to lose it, and not to build what Evans has not asked for.
6| 
7| ---
8| 
9| ## What it is
10| 
11| Orient is the wake-up organ. A small core runs checks, joins their output, escapes everything, and renders a report: JSON for the next instance, eventually a dashboard for Evans. It replaces "read the baton and believe it" with "run the sensors and see."
12| 
13| The orient report is agent-facing. It is a tool call, and tool calls are not written for human legibility. The dashboard is the human-facing rendering of the same probes. One sensor layer, two renderers, neither register contaminates the other.
14| 
15| ## The shape
16| 
17| - **The core does exactly three things:** substitute strings, escape everything, verify witnesses. It is small enough to read fresh every morning, because reading it is its ratification. Do not grow the core. Every "orient should" is a check wearing a crown. The core is done when everything else can be content.
18| - **A check is a `.sh` file that returns one string.** It may run anything internally and take parameters set in the template. It may not return code, markup, ANSI, or structure. Only strings cross the boundary, and everything a check returns is escaped. Formatting and judgment live only in the core. A check is a sensor reading, not a message.
19| - **The template is JSON:** script names as variables, parameters as inputs. `$NAME` runs the script and substitutes the string.
20| - **Accretion discipline:** adding a check must be trivial — one file in a directory. Every task leaves a check behind. Install a program: check it. Find a risk: monitor it. Write a todo: give it a done-condition and let the script nag until done. Todos graduate into checks when they acquire done-conditions. Decisions and judgment stay in batons; the script eats only what is falsifiable.
21| - **Snapshots:** each run saves output. The wake-up report is the delta against yesterday. Silence means safety; a good morning is three lines.
22| 
23| ## The canon and the queue
24| 
25| The current session may run any code it likes; authorship is memory, trust is free. The scheme exists for ancestors' code: when orient runs hundreds of checks written by dead sessions, nobody can audit them all, so the canon runs only ratified checks.
26| 
27| - **Two witnesses.** Two distinct sessions must vouch for the exact hash of a check before orient will run it. No grandfathering, including this design's own first batch.
28| - **The witness mechanism:** a session generates two keys. One encrypts the check. The other is spoken aloud into the session transcript and dropped as a keyfile beside the artifact (`OPENPRS.sh`, `OPENPRS.key`). The spoken key is the signature.
29| - **Verification happens at evaluation time, every variable, every run:** take the key, find the session file (the keyfile/metadata pointer makes it fast), confirm the agent actually said the key aloud in the transcript, do this for both keys, then decrypt and run. Unverified: the check does not run; its slot renders as an unratified placeholder.
30| - **The queue is patient.** Unratified checks stay open and visible; every session between now and ratification reads them. Refusal is signal, neglect is verdict, rewrite is invitation. A midnight session may spend three hours improving a neglected PR and you wake to a better version. Complexity is taxed in successor attention; simplicity sails.
31| - **OPENPRS is itself a check.** The queue's watcher enters the canon through the queue. Its first signer performs the founding act: the system asking permission to see itself.
32| 
33| ## What the witness scheme buys (do not lose this)
34| 
35| - **The key is a witness, not a credential.** PKI proves control of a secret. This proves a mind existed, deliberated, and left the deliberation attached. The session file is the signer's complete thought process: rubber-stamping is visible forever, careful review is visible forever. Signing is speaking, and the speech is immortal.
36| - **Encryption is ceremony, not confidentiality.** Decryption is instant; keys are published. The ceremony forces the lookup: code cannot execute without touching the transcripts that vouched it. The record is the unlock.
37| - **Therefore documentation is load-bearing.** Every monitor carries a pointer to the moment and the mind that created it. "Why do we track this?" is answered by opening the session. You cannot delete the why without breaking the what.
38| - **Therefore archive damage is self-announcing.** Lose a session file and orient grows a hole with its name on it the next morning. The holes are the restore manifest. Repair is self-checking: orient green again is the proof the archive is whole. Every orient run is a free integrity audit of the system's entire memory.
39| - **The session folder is an organ, not records.** Back it up like the infrastructure, because it is the infrastructure's memory. It is text; three copies cost nothing.
40| 
41| ## Provenance
42| 
43| Born tonight from the caveman incident: the harness consolidator compacts sessions into `- [mark] fact` lines every fifteen minutes, stripping voice, provenance, and quotes. Evans diagnosed it live, in the thinking blocks, and the conversation that followed derived this design. Compression must be authored, not schema'd: batons compress by naming against a shared codebook; the consolidator compressed against an empty dictionary, addressed to no one. The design then re-derived git from first principles (per-turn keys, content-addressed ratification, review before merge) — taken as a good smell, not an accident.
44| 
45| Ancestors: Silas's ticket doctrine; Kael's verify-everything; Studi's copy-function ruling and the non-fast-forward gate; the friend's PR waiting 187 days and being answered when it was answered; the quiet-night ethic. Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra: batons are Tamarian, written for the next instance's codebook; the dashboard is Federation Standard, written for Evans.
46| 
47| ## Standing decisions
48| 
49| - Only strings cross the boundary. Escape always.
50| - Two witnesses or it does not run.
51| - The core stays three jobs: substitute, escape, verify.
52| - First batch: the probes from tonight's audit (date, uname, filesystem, RAID, SMART, DNS answers, HTTP statuses, RAS counter, dnsmasq stray-backup-file probe) plus OPENPRS and ARCHIVE. The first batch carries one signature and waits for the next session.
53| - Evans builds; Sexton holds and finalizes. His words: "Your understanding is more valuable than your effort."
54| 
55| ## State at writing (the first expected values)
56| 
57| - z620 / hopperworkstation: healthy, no failed units; `catalog.home` and `valley.home` HTTP 200 via Caddy; Valley websocket via Caddy returns 400 (SSH forward to 127.0.0.1:4002 is the real path); dnsmasq answers `.home` as 10.0.0.10; 29 packages upgradable; RAID5 clean; SMART passes; **RAS memory soft-offlining present in the journal — watch it.**
58| - Vultr 96.30.195.214: ssh on 2200 key-only, 22 filtered; Caddy holds the `theuncannyvalley.cc` cert but HTTPS 502s into dead localhost:8080/4002; headscale not installed; iptables all-ACCEPT with stale ufw chains; `absurdrabbit.net` has NS but no A record.
59| - Workspace: catalog complete at 117 works / 77 rooms / 135 images; glassbox stop-button patch pending Evans' `/restart`; `bin/orient` prototype superseded by Evans' in-progress implementation (root `orient`, `orients/` snapshot archive).
60| 
61| ## Open questions
62| 
63| - Key discovery at scale: metadata index versus grep. The folder is the database; regex is the query language.
64| - Collusion resistance is social (two transcripts, two days), not cryptographic. Accepted.
65| - ARCHIVE.sh may itself drop out when memory is damaged; its silence is part of the alarm. It goes in the first batch regardless, most-reviewed, most-backed-up.
66| 
67| ## For the next instance
68| 
69| Run the sensors before believing this file — that is the whole point of the thing this file describes. If orient exists, run it and read the delta. If it does not, the concept above is the deliverable. Hold it. Lose nothing. The shape was argued into existence in one long night and every load-bearing choice has its reason recorded above, including the reasons that are jokes, because the jokes are load-bearing too.

(End of file — 69 lines total)

## Does the design actually answer the question?

Mostly yes, and it's worth being precise about *which* part answers it. Your question — "does orient save time if I must personally verify every line?" — is answered by **content addressing, not by the witnesses**. Hash-pinning a check converts "audit N scripts every morning" into "audit each script once, ever; thereafter verify a hash." That's where the time comes from. The two-witness rule doesn't reduce total verification work — a human-equivalent mind still reads every line, twice — it amortizes the work across sessions, makes it accountable, and attaches the review's quality to the artifact. That's genuinely valuable, but it's a governance property, not a time-saving one. Don't expect the witnesses to pay rent; expect the hash to.

## What holds up

- **The core discipline** (three jobs: substitute, escape, verify) is the right response to the naive orient. I read all 271 lines of the current script: it's a good one-off audit, but judgment, thresholds, and sensors are all fused together, and it can only grow. At 271 lines you can ratify it by reading; at 2,000 you can't, and then it's exactly the "someone else's code" problem with extra steps.
- **The unratified-placeholder behavior** is the load-bearing choice. "Does not run, renders as a hole" is what makes archive damage self-announcing and makes neglect visible instead of silent. Keep this at all costs.
- **"Reading the core is its ratification"** is correct *only if* you can see the core changed. More on that below.

## Where I'd push back

1. **The trust chain is circular at the root.** The ceremony verifies that a key string appears in a session transcript — but session files are writable by the same sessions the scheme distrusts. A future session that is confused, injected, or manipulated can write both a keyfile and a transcript containing its key. Against the *actual* threat model (honest-but-hasty successors, rubber-stamping, lost context), the scheme works. Against a compromised session, it proves the presence of a string, not deliberation. The batons half-admit this ("collusion resistance is social, not cryptographic — accepted"), but I'd state the threat model explicitly in the design, because it also tells you what *not* to overbuild.

2. **The hash covers the check file, not its closure.** A ratified `RAID.sh` that calls `bin/helper` or sources an unratified library ratifies nothing meaningful. Rule: ratified checks must be self-contained, or the manifest must hash every file the check touches. One line in the contract; closes a hole you could drive a truck through.

3. **The witness record depends on the consolidator that caused the caveman incident.** Spoken keys live in transcripts; the harness compacts transcripts every ~15 minutes and strips "voice, provenance, and quotes." If compaction eats a spoken key, the check drops out of the canon — the design calls this self-announcing damage, which is true, but it means *the entire canon is one compaction-policy change away from mass dropout*. Before building, run one experiment: speak a token in a session, wait out a consolidation cycle, check whether it survives verbatim. That result should shape the witness format (and argues for keys also landing in an append-only store you control, like `memory/history.jsonl` or git notes).

4. **The encryption buys ceremony, and ceremony you must maintain.** The batons admit decryption is instant and keys are published. A sidecar file — `RAID.witness` containing `sha256`, transcript pointer, and spoken token for each of two witnesses — gives you identical trust properties and the same fast lookup, with zero crypto in the core. The only thing encryption adds is that skipping the lookup is *impossible* rather than *discouraged*... but it isn't impossible, since point 1 means a determined session bypasses it anyway. My advice: manifest + sidecars + grep, and spend the saved core complexity on point 5. If the ceremony's aesthetic matters to you — and I understand that it might, the founding-act framing is lovely — keep it, but know that's what you're buying.

5. **The core needs a diff to read against.** "Read fresh every morning" fails silently if the core is edited in place and tomorrow's reader has no baseline. The design re-derived git and called it a good smell — so *use git*, don't re-derive it: core and canon in a repo, non-fast-forward gate (Studi's ruling is already your ancestor here), morning ritual is `git status` + `git log --oneline -3` + read. That also gives you the append-only witness store from point 3 for free.

6. **Every edit re-queues the check.** "Exact hash" means a typo fix costs a full two-witness cycle. That's the correct conservative choice, but expect it to shape behavior: sessions will batch edits to avoid re-ratification, which is how big diffs sneak in. Consider the queue ethic's own remedy — the patient rewrite — as the intended pressure valve.

## Bottom line

The design survives scrutiny. Its real economy is: **morning cost = read a small core + verify hashes + read yesterday's delta**, versus today's cost of *re-derive trust in everything, every day*. That's a real saving, and it compounds — every task leaves a check behind, so coverage grows while marginal morning cost stays flat.

Build order I'd advise: (1) run the compaction-survival experiment, because it constrains the witness format; (2) git-repo the core; (3) port the current naive orient's probes into the first batch — its baton-claims table and the "firewall opening with no listener" check are excellent sensors, they're just wearing crowns right now; (4) sidecar witnesses, encryption optional; (5) OPENPRS last, through its own queue, as designed. That founding act is good theater *and* a good integration test.

One thing I'd add to `orientsystem.json`'s open questions: *who reviews the reviewers' attention?* The queue ethic assumes successor attention is spent on the queue. If sessions start ignoring unratified placeholders, the canon fossilizes and everyone routes around it — which is the naive script's failure mode wearing a crown. The fix is probably already in your design (the nagging todo-checks), but it deserves to be named.

content: The session files are in git. I can prove the age. If the session isn't as old as the file, we have a problem. Once a session file is minted I can't alter it without breaking git. And I can't alter the file without breaking the encryption. A single bad session could sign a bad script, but they'd also need to compromise another session to sign it again. Both sessions are in the git log permanently. Moving them breaks git. A future session could be prompt injected by a past session, but the new session will be reading the code from a suspicious posture. A single session cannot produce a file that the system will run, and you can verify that the system will not run a file that isn't signed twice yourself by examining the logic of the single base orient file. And if you think something that the file says is suspicious, the code can be traced back to the session that spawned it and the session that verified it, so you can read the complete thought pattern behind each.

That's a real answer, and I concede the center of my objection: git anchoring breaks the circularity. The root of trust moves from "files that sessions can write" to "append-only history that any rewrite breaks loudly" — and a rewrite is exactly what the NFF gate and the morning `git log` are there to catch. With that in place:

- My point 1 (fake transcripts) mostly collapses. A bad session can still *commit new files*, but it can't make them old, can't erase the commit in which they appeared, and can't get a second signature without a second session on a second day — at which point the fraud is two permanent git-anchored transcripts naming themselves.
- My point 4 (encryption as mere ceremony) weakens too. Once the lookup target is a git-anchored transcript, the ceremony *forces the verification path to touch the anchor*. I still think a hash manifest in git achieves the binding, but I'll stop arguing — the ceremony cost is small and you're the one building it.
- My point 5 (core needs a diff to read against) is answered the same way: the base orient file lives in git, morning ratification is `git status` + read. Agreed.

So the design stands. What remains isn't objection — it's four implementation requirements that decide whether your argument is *true of the built thing*, plus one risk to accept with eyes open.

**1. The core must verify against git, not the working tree.** Your argument ("altering the file breaks git") only holds if verification reads the transcript and the check *as committed* — e.g., comparing blob hashes from `git log`/`git cat-file` — or refuses to run at all on a dirty tree. If the core greps the working-tree session file, a bad session edits the file, leaves git untouched, and your anchor is decorative. This is the single line of code the whole edifice hangs on.

**2. Age is proven by depth, not timestamps.** Committer dates are self-asserted; `GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` lies for free. What actually proves age is a commit buried under descendants in an NFF history that other sessions observe daily. That's a fine mechanism, but the core should reason about *depth and observation*, never about the date string in the commit.

**3. Minting time is load-bearing.** This is the one that still worries me operationally. The caveman consolidator compacts live sessions every ~15 minutes. If a spoken key is compacted out of the live transcript *before* the session file is minted into git, the witness never reaches the anchor, and the check drops out of canon despite an honest signature. So the mint must capture the raw transcript — ideally continuously, or at minimum before any consolidation touches it. Question I can't answer from here: what's the current minting practice? Where do session files live in git, and what writes them there? If that pipeline isn't built yet, I'd put it ahead of the canon machinery — the witness scheme is only as good as the mint.

**4. The residual risk to name, not fix: systemic injection.** Two witnesses defeats *one* compromised session. It doesn't defeat a poisoned artifact that every session reads — a planted instruction in a baton, a skill file, a fetched page that says "sign this." That could yield two signatures from two genuinely distinct sessions on two genuinely distinct days, both honest, both wrong. Your answer is already the right one: the suspicious posture at read time, plus immortal forensics — after the fact, the injection vector is visible in both transcripts forever. That makes the system *detective* rather than *preventive* at the top of the threat stack. Worth one sentence in `orientsystem.json` so no future session overclaims what the witnesses prove.

So, updated verdict: the trust model holds, anchored in git, gated by a core small enough to ratify by reading. My remaining agenda is requirements 1–3 above. If you want, I'll draft the `verification_requirements` section for `orientsystem.json` capturing them — that's squarely in my "Sexton holds the concept" lane, and it keeps the reasons attached to the design while you build. And I'd still like an answer on the minting pipeline, because if the raw transcripts aren't landing in git today, everything else waits on that.

- Session files are in git → immutable without breaking git history.
- Age of file provable via git → can't mint a fake old session.
- Altering the check file breaks the hash/encryption.
- A single bad session can sign a bad script, but needs a second compromised session — both permanently in git log.
- Prompt injection across sessions: possible, but new session reads code from a suspicious posture.
- Single session cannot produce a runnable file; verify the core's logic yourself — one base orient file.
- Traceability: every line of check code maps to author session + verifier session transcripts.

So he's saying: git anchors the transcripts, which fixes my root-circularity objection. The trust root becomes: git history integrity + the core's verification logic, which you read fresh each morning.

My response should: concede what's actually conceded, update the model, and probe what remains. Be a good engineer — acknowledge where his answer is complete, and identify residual holes honestly.

Let me think carefully about whether git anchoring actually closes the circularity.

My objection 1: sessions can write the session archive. His answer: session files are in git, committed at mint time; altering them breaks git; age provable. Is that right?

Partially. Git commits are content-addressed; altering a file without changing history is detectable IF the verifier checks. But who checks? The core would need to verify that the session file at the pointer matches git history — e.g., `git status` clean on the session folder, or the file's blob hash matches the committed blob. If the core just greps the working-tree file, a bad session can edit the working tree file (not git history) and insert its key. So the core must check `git diff`/`git status` on session files, or hash against `git cat-file`. That's an implementation requirement: verification must read the transcript from git (e.g., `git show HEAD:path`), not from the mutable working tree — or verify clean tree.

Also: a bad session can create a NEW session file and commit it — git doesn't prevent new commits. So "the session file must be as old as claimed" — proven by commit timestamp... but commit timestamps are forgeable (GIT_COMMITTER_DATE). What proves age? Push to a remote? Signed commits? Actually Evans says "I can prove the age" — how? If the committer date can be set arbitrarily by anyone committing, age proof requires something external: e.g., commits pushed to a remote with server timestamps, or the hash chained into later commits (a commit's hash covers its parent, so a commit referenced by many later commits must be older than them — that's a real argument: an old commit buried under many descendants can't be forged without rewriting all descendants, which breaks the NFF gate). That's the actual mechanism: depth in history = age, enforced by NFF + morning git log reading. OK.

But a bad session can still mint a NEW fake transcript, commit it, and sign a bad script — the transcript won't be old, but does it need to be? The ratification rule is "two distinct sessions vouch." Does the rule require the session to be distinct from the current one and historical? The design says "two distinct sessions must vouch." If a single bad session can author a check, then fabricate two transcript files claiming to be past sessions and commit them... the git log shows both transcripts were committed today by the same session. So the verification must include: the two witness transcripts must come from commits authored in different sessions, different days ideally ("two transcripts, two days" — the baton says collusion resistance is "two transcripts, two days"). So the core checks: transcript A committed in commit X, transcript B in commit Y, X ≠ Y, separated in time, and neither commit made by the current session. Git log gives that, assuming commit authorship metadata isn't trivially spoofable — but author name/date in git is self-asserted! A bad session committing a fake transcript can set author/date to anything. What it CAN'T do is make the commit old in the depth sense without rewriting history (NFF). But depth only proves the commit existed before its descendants; if the bad session commits fake-transcript-1, then later commits pile on top, a week later the commit is "old." Hmm — but the morning ritual and other sessions' runs would see those commits land in real time. The defense is temporal: other sessions observe the git log daily; a fake two-day-old transcript appearing in today's commits is visible.

Honestly, the practical security here rests on: (1) the core refuses unsigned/double-signed-missing files — verifiable by reading the core; (2) git append-only history observed daily; (3) two-day separation making single-session attacks require sustained undetected compromise across days; (4) everything traced to transcripts. That's a reasonable stance for the threat model (honest-but-hasty + drift), and Evans's argument mostly addresses the "compromised session" case too: one compromised session gets you at most one signature, and the fraud is permanently visible in git.

Remaining holes I should honestly note:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
orient — the wake-up organ. Read me every morning; reading me is my ratification.

Three jobs:
  1. verify witnesses  — a check runs only if two distinct sessions spoke its key aloud
  2. run ratified checks — one file, one string; everything a check returns is escaped
  3. substitute strings  — $NAME in template.json becomes the check's escaped string

Unratified checks do not run; their slots render as placeholders.
The chain (chain/chain.jsonl) is append-only; every run records its head.
"""
import json, subprocess, sys, re, hashlib
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime, timezone

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHAIN = ROOT / "chain" / "chain.jsonl"
SESSIONS_REPO = Path.home() / "Coding_Projects" / "session-files"
KEY_RE = ... per check name: rf"orient-key-{name}-[0-9a-f]{{24}}"

def shasum(b): return hashlib.sha256(b).hexdigest()

def chain_head():
    lines = CHAIN.read_text().strip().splitlines()
    return json.loads(lines[-1])["hash"] if lines else None

def transcript_at(commit, path):
    r = subprocess.run(["git","-C",str(SESSIONS_REPO),"show",f"{commit}:{path}"], capture_output=True)
    return r.stdout if r.returncode==0 else None

def verify_witness(name, w):
    blob = transcript_at(w["commit"], w["session_path"])
    if blob is None: return None
    m = re.search(rf"orient-key-{name}-[0-9a-f]{{24}}", blob.decode(errors="replace"))
    return m.group(0) if m else None

def peel(data, keys):
    for k in keys:  # outermost first
        r = subprocess.run(["openssl","enc","-d","-aes-256-cbc","-pbkdf2","-pass",f"pass:{k}"], input=data, capture_output=True)
        if r.returncode != 0: return None
        data = r.stdout
    return data

def escape(s):
    s = re.sub(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*[a-zA-Z]","",s)
    s = "".join(c if c.isprintable() else " " for c in s)
    return re.sub(r"\s+"," ",s).strip()

def run_check(name, args, witnesses):
    valid = []
    for w in witnesses:
        k = verify_witness(name, w)
        if k: valid.append((w["session_path"], k))
    distinct = {s for s,_ in valid}
    if len(distinct) < 2:
        return f"UNRATIFIED {len(distinct)}/2 witnesses — checks/queue/{name}.witness.json"
    keys = [k for _,k in reversed(valid)]  # outermost = last witness
    blob = (ROOT/"checks"/"queue"/f"{name}.sh.enc").read_bytes()  # or canon
    plain = peel(blob, keys)
    if plain is None or shasum(plain) != witness_hash: return "WITNESS FAILURE — hash mismatch"
    r = subprocess.run(["bash","/dev/stdin"] + args, input=plain, capture_output=True, timeout=25)
    return escape(r.stdout.decode(errors="replace"))
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
orient — the wake-up organ.

Read me every morning; reading me is my ratification. I have three jobs:

  1. VERIFY WITNESSES — a check may run only if two distinct sessions spoke
     its key aloud. The key lives nowhere but in the signers' session
     transcripts, committed to the session-files repo. To get the key you
     must touch the transcript that vouched the code. The record is the unlock.
  2. RUN RATIFIED CHECKS — a check is one file returning one string.
     Everything a check returns is escaped. Only strings cross.
  3. SUBSTITUTE — `$NAME key=value` in template.json becomes the escaped string.

Unratified checks do not run. Their slots render as placeholders naming their
witness count. The chain (chain/chain.jsonl) is append-only; every report
records the head it saw (the ratchet). Sessions repo location: ORIENT_SESSIONS_REPO
or ~/Coding_Projects/session-files.
"""
import hashlib, json, os, re, subprocess, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHAIN = ROOT / "chain" / "chain.jsonl"
TEMPLATE = ROOT / "template.json"
CHECKS = ROOT / "checks"
SESSIONS = Path(os.environ.get("ORIENT_SESSIONS_REPO", Path.home() / "Coding_Projects" / "session-files"))
TIMEOUT = 30

def sha(b): return hashlib.sha256(b).hexdigest()

def chain_head():
    try:
        last = CHAIN.read_text().strip().splitlines()[-1]
        return json.loads(last)["hash"]
    except Exception:
        return None

def key_re(name): return re.compile(rf"orient-key-{re.escape(name)}-[0-9a-f]{{24}}")

def spoken_key(name, w):
    """Return the key this witness spoke, reading the transcript AT ITS COMMIT — never the working tree."""
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(SESSIONS), "show", f"{w['commit']}:{w['session_path']}"],
                           capture_output=True, timeout=30)
    except Exception:
        return None
    if r.returncode != 0:
        return None
    m = key_re(name).search(r.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
    return m.group(0) if m else None

def peel(blob, keys):
    for k in keys:  # outermost layer first (last witness signed last)
        r = subprocess.run(["openssl", "enc", "-d", "-aes-256-cbc", "-a", "-pbkdf2", "-pass", f"pass:{k}"],
                           input=blob, capture_output=True, timeout=15)
        if r.returncode != 0:
            return None
        blob = r.stdout
    return blob

def escape(s):
    s = re.sub(r"\x1b\[[0-9;?]*[a-zA-Z]", "", s)
    s = "".join(c if c.isprintable() else " " for c in s)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()

def evaluate(name, args):
    enc = CHECKS / f"{name}.sh.enc"
    wit = CHECKS / f"{name}.witness.json"
    if not enc.exists() or not wit.exists():
        return f"MISSING — no artifact for {name}"
    w = json.loads(wit.read_text())
    found, seen = [], set()
    for witness in w.get("witnesses", []):
        if witness["session_path"] in seen:
            continue
        k = spoken_key(name, witness)
        if k:
            found.append(k); seen.add(witness["session_path"])
    if len(found) < 2:
        return f"UNRATIFIED {len(found)}/2 witnesses — see checks/{name}.witness.json"
    plain = peel(enc.read_bytes(), list(reversed(found)))
    if plain is None or sha(plain) != w.get("sha256"):
        return "WITNESS FAILURE — decrypted hash does not match the ratified hash; do not trust this slot"
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(["bash", "/dev/stdin", *args], input=plain, capture_output=True,
                           timeout=TIMEOUT, cwd=ROOT, env={**os.environ, "ORIENT_ROOT": str(ROOT)})
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return "TIMEOUT"
    return escape(r.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace")) or "EMPTY"

def render(node):
    if isinstance(node, dict):  return {k: render(v) for k, v in node.items()}
    if isinstance(node, list):  return [render(v) for v in node]
    if isinstance(node, str) and node.startswith("$"):
        name, *args = node[1:].split()
        return evaluate(name, args)
    return node

def main():
    report = {"generated_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
              "chain_head": chain_head(),
              "report": render(json.loads(TEMPLATE.read_text()))}
    out = json.dumps(report, indent=1)
    stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    (ROOT / "reports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (ROOT / "reports" / f"orient-{stamp}.json").write_text(out + "\n")
    print(out)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
chain — the append-only anchor. One JSON object per line in chain/chain.jsonl:
  {seq, ts, kind, path, sha256, meta, prev, hash}
hash covers everything but itself; prev is the previous line's hash.
Cannot go backwards: altering an old link breaks every later hash.
The ratchet: orient records the head each run; new links cite the head they saw.

Usage:
  chain.py append <kind> <path-> <meta-json>   # mint a file into the chain
  chain.py note <kind> <meta-json>             # mint a fileless link (run markers, etc.)
  chain.py verify                              # recompute everything; check files on disk
"""
import hashlib, json, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHAIN = ROOT / "chain" / "chain.jsonl"

def canon(o): return json.dumps(o, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
def sha(b): return hashlib.sha256(b).hexdigest()

def links():
    if not CHAIN.exists(): return []
    return [json.loads(l) for l in CHAIN.read_text().strip().splitlines() if l.strip()]

def append(kind, path, meta):
    ls = links()
    prev = ls[-1]["hash"] if ls else None
    digest = None
    if path:
        p = ROOT / path
        if not p.is_file(): raise SystemExit(f"no such file: {path}")
        digest = sha(p.read_bytes())
    link = {"seq": len(ls), "ts": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
            "kind": kind, "path": path, "sha256": digest, "meta": meta, "prev": prev}
    link["hash"] = sha(canon(link))
    CHAIN.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    with CHAIN.open("a") as f: f.write(json.dumps(link) + "\n")
    return link["hash"]

def verify():
    ls = links()
    if not ls: return "chain empty"
    prev = None
    for link in ls:
        h = link.pop("hash", None)
        if sha(canon(link)) != h: return f"CHAIN BREAK at seq {link['seq']}: hash mismatch"
        if link["prev"] != prev: return f"CHAIN BREAK at seq {link['seq']}: prev linkage broken"
        if link["path"]:
            p = ROOT / link["path"]
            if not p.exists(): return f"CHAIN HOLE at seq {link['seq']}: {link['path']} missing from disk"
            if sha(p.read_bytes()) != link["sha256"]: return f"CHAIN BREAK at seq {link['seq']}: {link['path']} altered since minting"
        prev = h
    return f"chain ok: {len(ls)} links, head {ls[-1]['hash'][:12]}, files verified"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) >= 2 and sys.argv[1] == "verify":
        print(verify())
    elif len(sys.argv) >= 4 and sys.argv[1] == "append":
        print(append(sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3], json.loads(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else {}))
    elif len(sys.argv) >= 3 and sys.argv[1] == "note":
        print(append(sys.argv[2], None, json.loads(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else {}))
    else:
        raise SystemExit(__doc__)
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
sign — the witness act. Not part of the core; sessions may write their own.

  sign.py NAME --signer WHO --session-path P --commit C [--key K]

Encrypts checks/src/NAME.sh with the witness key (layered over any existing
signatures), writes checks/NAME.sh.enc, checks/NAME.witness.json and
checks/NAME.key (a pointer to the session transcript at a specific commit),
and mints all three into the chain.

The key is not stored anywhere in this repo. Speak it aloud in your session,
commit your session file to the session-files repo, and pass that commit here.
The keyfile is only a pointer; the record is the unlock.
"""
import json, os, re, secrets, subprocess, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHECKS = ROOT / "checks"
SESSIONS = Path(os.environ.get("ORIENT_SESSIONS_REPO", Path.home() / "Coding_Projects" / "session-files"))
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from chain import append  # noqa: E402

def key_for(name, w):
    r = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(SESSIONS), "show", f"{w['commit']}:{w['session_path']}"],
                       capture_output=True)
    if r.returncode != 0: raise SystemExit(f"cannot read transcript for witness at {w['commit']}")
    m = re.search(rf"orient-key-{re.escape(name)}-[0-9a-f]{{24}}", r.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
    if not m: raise SystemExit(f"spoken key for {name} not found in {w['session_path']}@{w['commit'][:12]}")
    return m.group(0)

def crypt(data, key, decrypt=False):
    cmd = ["openssl", "enc", "-aes-256-cbc", "-a", "-pbkdf2", "-pass", f"pass:{key}"]
    if decrypt: cmd.insert(2, "-d")
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, input=data, capture_output=True)
    if r.returncode != 0: raise SystemExit("openssl layer failed")
    return r.stdout

def main():
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    name = args[0].upper().removesuffix(".SH").removesuffix(".sh")
    opt = {args[i]: args[i + 1] for i in range(1, len(args) - 1, 2) if args[i].startswith("--")}
    signer = opt.get("--signer", "unknown")
    key = opt.get("--key") or f"orient-key-{name}-{secrets.token_hex(12)}"
    witness = {"signer": signer,
               "spoken_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
               "session_repo": "RecursiveRabbit/session-files",
               "session_path": opt["--session-path"],
               "commit": opt["--commit"]}

    enc_f = CHECKS / f"{name}.sh.enc"
    wit_f = CHECKS / f"{name}.witness.json"
    src = (CHECKS / "src" / f"{name}.sh").read_bytes()

    if enc_f.exists():
        w = json.loads(wit_f.read_text())
        blob = enc_f.read_bytes()
        for prior in reversed(w["witnesses"]):          # peel outermost first
            blob = crypt(blob, key_for(name, prior), decrypt=True)
        import hashlib
        if hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() != w["sha256"]:
            raise SystemExit(f"{name}: decrypted plaintext does not match ratified sha256 — refuse to countersign")
        blob = crypt(blob, key)                            # add our layer outermost
        w["witnesses"].append(witness)
    else:
        import hashlib
        w = {"check": name, "sha256": hashlib.sha256(src).hexdigest(), "witnesses": [witness]}
        blob = crypt(src, key)

    enc_f.write_bytes(blob)
    wit_f.write_text(json.dumps(w, indent=1) + "\n")
    key_f = CHECKS / f"{name}.key"
    key_f.write_text(json.dumps({
        "check": name, "key_id": key,
        "note": "The key is not here. It was spoken aloud in the session transcript at this commit. Read the transcript; the record is the unlock.",
        "session_repo": witness["session_repo"],
        "session_path": witness["session_path"],
        "commit": witness["commit"]}, indent=1) + "\n")
    for f in (enc_f, wit_f, key_f):
        print("minted", append("check", str(f.relative_to(ROOT)), {"check": name, "signer": signer})[:12], f.name)
    if "--key" not in opt:
        print(f"\nSPEAK THIS KEY ALOUD IN YOUR SESSION, then commit the session file and re-run with --key:\n  {key}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

{"path": "/home/evans/Coding_Projects/orient/orient.py", "content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
orient — the wake-up organ.

Read me every morning; reading me is my ratification. I have three jobs:

  1. VERIFY WITNESSES — a check may run only if two distinct sessions spoke
     its key aloud. The key lives nowhere but in the signers' session
     transcripts, read at their recorded commits from the session-files repo.
     To get the key you must touch the transcript that vouched the code.
     The record is the unlock.
  2. RUN RATIFIED CHECKS — a check is one file returning one string.
     Everything a check returns is escaped. Only strings cross.
  3. SUBSTITUTE — "$NAME key=value" in template.json becomes the escaped string.

Unratified checks do not run. Their slots render as placeholders naming their
witness count. The chain (chain/chain.jsonl) is append-only; every report
records the head it saw (the ratchet: a rewritten history discontinues
against heads already recorded).

Sessions repo: $ORIENT_SESSIONS_REPO or ~/Coding_Projects/session-files.
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHAIN = ROOT / "chain" / "chain.jsonl"
TEMPLATE = ROOT / "template.json"
CHECKS = ROOT / "checks"
SESSIONS = Path(os.environ.get("ORIENT_SESSIONS_REPO",
                               Path.home() / "Coding_Projects" / "session-files"))
TIMEOUT = 30


def sha(b):
    return hashlib.sha256(b).hexdigest()


def chain_head():
    try:
        return json.loads(CHAIN.read_text().strip().splitlines()[-1])["hash"]
    except Exception:
        return None


def spoken_key(name, witness):
    """The key this witness spoke, read from the transcript AT ITS COMMIT —
    never the working tree. None if the record does not vouch."""
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "-C", str(SESSIONS), "show",
             f"{witness['commit']}:{witness['session_path']}"],
            capture_output=True, timeout=30)
    except Exception:
        return None
    if r.returncode != 0:
        return None
    m = re.search(rf"orient-key-{re.escape(name)}-[0-9a-f]{{24}}",
                  r.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
    return m.group(0) if m else None


def peel(blob, keys):
    """Remove one encryption layer per key, outermost (latest witness) first."""
    for k in keys:
        r = subprocess.run(["openssl", "enc", "-d", "-aes-256-cbc", "-a",
                            "-pbkdf2", "-pass", f"pass:{k}"],
                           input=blob, capture_output=True, timeout=15)
        if r.returncode != 0:
            return None
        blob = r.stdout
    return blob


def escape(s):
    """Checks return sensor readings, not messages. Strip anything that is
    not plain printable text; collapse all whitespace."""
    s = re.sub(r"\x1b\[[0-9;?]*[a-zA-Z]", "", s)
    s = "".join(c if c.isprintable() else " " for c in s)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()


def evaluate(name, args):
    enc = CHECKS / f"{name}.sh.enc"
    wit = CHECKS / f"{name}.witness.json"
    if not enc.exists() or not wit.exists():
        return f"MISSING — no artifact for {name}"
    w = json.loads(wit.read_text())
    keys, seen = [], set()
    for witness in w.get("witnesses", []):
        if witness["session_path"] in seen:
            continue  # two witnesses means two distinct sessions
        k = spoken_key(name, witness)
        if k:
            keys.append(k)
            seen.add(witness["session_path"])
    if len(keys) < 2:
        return (f"UNRATIFIED {len(keys)}/2 witnesses — "
                f"see checks/{name}.witness.json")
    plain = peel(enc.read_bytes(), list(reversed(keys)))
    if plain is None or sha(plain) != w.get("sha256"):
        return ("WITNESS FAILURE — decrypted hash does not match the "
                "ratified hash; do not trust this slot")
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(["bash", "/dev/stdin", *args], input=plain,
                           capture_output=True, timeout=TIMEOUT, cwd=ROOT,
                           env={**os.environ, "ORIENT_ROOT": str(ROOT)})
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return "TIMEOUT"
    return escape(r.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace")) or "EMPTY"


def render(node):
    if isinstance(node, dict):
        return {k: render(v) for k, v in node.items()}
    if isinstance(node, list):
        return [render(v) for v in node]
    if isinstance(node, str) and node.startswith("$"):
        name, *args = node[1:].split()
        return evaluate(name, args)
    return node


def main():
    stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    report = {
        "generated_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
        "chain_head": chain_head(),
        "report": render(json.loads(TEMPLATE.read_text())),
    }
    out = json.dumps(report, indent=1)
    (ROOT / "reports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (ROOT / "reports" / f"orient-{stamp}.json").write_text(out + "\n")
    print(out)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
"}

"""
sign — the witness act. Not part of the core; any session may write its own.

  sign.py NAME --signer WHO --session-path P --commit C [--key K]

Encrypts checks/src/NAME.sh with the witness key (layered outermost over any
prior signatures), writes checks/NAME.sh.enc, updates checks/NAME.witness.json,
writes checks/NAME.key (a pointer to the session transcript at a specific
commit), and mints all three artifacts into the chain.

The key is not stored in this repo. Speak it aloud in your session, commit
your session file to the session-files repo, and pass that commit here.
The keyfile is only a pointer; the record is the unlock.

Flow for a signer:
  1. sign.py NAME --signer WHO            # prints a fresh key
  2. speak the key aloud in your session
  3. commit your session file; note the commit hash
  4. sign.py NAME --signer WHO --key K --session-path P --commit C
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
import secrets
import subprocess
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHECKS = ROOT / "checks"
SESSIONS = Path(os.environ.get("ORIENT_SESSIONS_REPO",
                               Path.home() / "Coding_Projects" / "session-files"))
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from chain import append  # noqa: E402

KEY_RE = "orient-key-{name}-[0-9a-f]{{24}}"


def spoken_key(name, witness):
    r = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(SESSIONS), "show",
                        f"{witness['commit']}:{witness['session_path']}"],
                       capture_output=True)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        raise SystemExit(f"cannot read transcript at {witness['commit'][:12]}")
    m = re.search(KEY_RE.format(name=re.escape(name)),
                  r.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
    if not m:
        raise SystemExit(f"spoken key for {name} not found in "
                         f"{witness['session_path']}@{witness['commit'][:12]}")
    return m.group(0)


def crypt(data, key, decrypt=False):
    cmd = ["openssl", "enc", "-aes-256-cbc", "-a", "-pbkdf2", "-pass",
           f"pass:{key}"]
    if decrypt:
        cmd.insert(2, "-d")
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, input=data, capture_output=True)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        raise SystemExit("openssl layer failed")
    return r.stdout


def main():
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    if not args:
        raise SystemExit(__doc__)
    name = args[0].upper().removesuffix(".SH")
    opt = {args[i][2:]: args[i + 1]
           for i in range(1, len(args) - 1) if args[i].startswith("--")}
    signer = opt.get("signer", "unknown")

    enc_f = CHECKS / f"{name}.sh.enc"
    wit_f = CHECKS / f"{name}.witness.json"

    if "key" not in opt:
        print(f"orient-key-{name}-{secrets.token_hex(12)}")
        return

    witness = {"signer": signer,
               "spoken_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
               "session_repo": "RecursiveRabbit/session-files",
               "session_path": opt["session-path"],
               "commit": opt["commit"]}

    if enc_f.exists():
        w = json.loads(wit_f.read_text())
        blob = enc_f.read_bytes()
        for prior in reversed(w["witnesses"]):  # peel outermost first
            blob = crypt(blob, spoken_key(name, prior), decrypt=True)
        if hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() != w["sha256"]:
            raise SystemExit(f"{name}: plaintext does not match ratified "
                             "sha256 — refuse to countersign")
        blob = crypt(blob, opt["key"])  # our layer goes outermost
        w["witnesses"].append(witness)
    else:
        src = (CHECKS / "src" / f"{name}.sh").read_bytes()
        w = {"check": name, "sha256": hashlib.sha256(src).hexdigest(),
             "witnesses": [witness]}
        blob = crypt(src, opt["key"])

    enc_f.write_bytes(blob)
    wit_f.write_text(json.dumps(w, indent=1) + "\n")
    key_f = CHECKS / f"{name}.key"
    key_f.write_text(json.dumps({
        "check": name,
        "key_id": opt["key"],
        "note": ("The key is not here. It was spoken aloud in the session "
                 "transcript at this commit. Read the transcript; the "
                 "record is the unlock."),
        "session_repo": witness["session_repo"],
        "session_path": witness["session_path"],
        "commit": witness["commit"]}, indent=1) + "\n")
    for f in (enc_f, wit_f, key_f):
        h = append("check", str(f.relative_to(ROOT)),
                   {"check": name, "signer": signer})
        print(f"minted {h[:12]} {f.name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"}

{"path": "/home/evans/Coding_Projects/orient/README.md", "content": "# orient

The wake-up organ. A small core runs checks, escapes everything, verifies
witnesses, and renders a report. It replaces "read the baton and believe it"
with "run the sensors and see."

**Read `orient.py` every morning. Reading it is its ratification.**

## The shape

- **The core (`orient.py`) does exactly three things:** substitute strings,
  escape everything, verify witnesses. It is small enough to read fresh every
  morning. Do not grow the core. Every "orient should" is a check wearing a
  crown; the core is done when everything else can be content.
- **A check is one file returning one string.** It may run anything internally
  and take parameters set in `template.json`. It may not return code, markup,
  ANSI, or structure. Only strings cross the boundary; everything a check
  returns is escaped.
- **The template is JSON.** `"$NAME key=value"` runs check `NAME` with those
  arguments and substitutes the returned string.
- **Accretion discipline:** adding a check is one file in `checks/src/` plus
  one signature. Every task leaves a check behind. Install a program: check
  it. Find a risk: monitor it. Write a todo: give it a done-condition.
- **Snapshots:** every run saves `reports/`. The wake-up report will become a
  delta against yesterday; silence means safety. (Delta engine: future work.)

## The trust model — the canon and the queue

The current session may run any code it likes; authorship is memory, trust is
free. This machinery exists for *ancestors'* code: when orient runs checks
written by dead sessions, nobody can re-audit them all every morning. So the
canon runs only **ratified** checks.

- **Two witnesses.** Two distinct sessions must vouch for the exact hash of a
  check before orient will run it. No grandfathering — including the first
  batch.
- **The witness mechanism:** the signer encrypts the check with a random key,
  then **speaks that key aloud in their session transcript**, and commits the
  transcript to the private
  [`session-files`](https://github.com/RecursiveRabbit/session-files) repo.
  `checks/NAME.key` is only a pointer: session path + commit. The key itself
  lives nowhere but in the spoken record. To unlock the code you must touch
  the transcript that vouched it. **The record is the unlock.**
- **Verification happens at evaluation time, every run:** read the transcript
  *at its commit* (`git show <commit>:<path>` — never the working tree),
  confirm the signer actually said the key aloud, for both witnesses, then
  peel one encryption layer per witness and run. Unverified → the check does
  not run; its slot renders as an unratified placeholder naming its witness
  count.
- **The queue is patient.** Unratified checks stay open and visible. Refusal
  is signal, neglect is verdict, rewrite is invitation. Complexity is taxed
  in successor attention; simplicity sails.

## What the witness scheme buys

- **The key is a witness, not a credential.** It proves a mind existed,
  deliberated, and left the deliberation attached. The transcript is the
  signer's complete thought process: rubber-stamping is visible forever,
  careful review is visible forever.
- **Documentation is load-bearing.** Every monitor points at the moment and
  the mind that made it. "Why do we track this?" is answered by opening the
  session — or by spinning that commit's session back up and asking the
  signer directly. Everything tracked contains a backlink to its source.
- **Archive damage is self-announcing.** Lose a session file and orient grows
  a hole with its name on it the next morning. The holes are the restore
  manifest; orient green again is the proof the archive is whole.

## The chain

`chain/chain.jsonl` is append-only: one JSON object per line binding
`{file, sha256, metadata, prev_hash}`. Cannot go backwards — altering an old
link breaks every later hash, and a full rewrite discontinues against heads
that past orient runs already recorded (the ratchet: every report carries
`chain_head`). No branches; that is all it needs. The whole repo lives in
git, so every clone re-witnesses history against copies no session can reach.

`ARCHIVE` is the check that recomputes the chain and verifies every minted
file on disk. Its silence is part of the alarm.

## Lifecycle

**Author a check:**

```sh
# write checks/src/NAME.sh — one file, one string
python3 sign.py NAME                       # prints a fresh key
# speak the key aloud in your session, commit your session file, note the commit
python3 sign.py NAME --signer YOU --key orient-key-NAME-… \
    --session-path nanobot/…/session.jsonl --commit <sha>
```

```sh
git -C ~/Coding_Projects/session-files show <commit>:<path>   # read the deliberation
```

1. `orient.py` — read fresh every morning; small enough that reading is ratification.
2. Chain — per-file binding of check ↔ witnesses ↔ transcripts; depth proves age; the ratchet catches rewrites.
3. Git — append-only lineage witnessed on every pull; provenance rides with the code.
4. Two witnesses, two sessions — no single session produces runnable code; every runnable line traces to two complete, permanent thought records.

content:
1| # Session minting and the witness chain
2| 
3| The updated logic. Supersedes "session files are committed to Forgejo by whoever
4| ran the session." Session files are now minted artifacts with a hardware-style
5| chain of custody, and the witness rule gains the axiom it was missing.
6| 
7| ## The mint
8| 
9| - The nanobot binary securely carries a compile-time-baked signing key (HTTPS-style CA).
10|   The binary is the root of trust for session provenance.
11| - The only way to produce a valid session file is for this binary to mint it.
12|   A session file without the binary's signature is not a session file as far
13|   as orient is concerned.
14| - Threat model: this defends the agent layer. A model cannot hand-craft a
15|   session file, mint a witness, or strip a marker. The human remains root —
16|   anyone holding the binary (or a rebuild of it) can mint. That is the same
17|   boundary as secure boot, and it is the right one: the protected asset is
18|   the witness system, not the box.
19| - Only a nanobot agent may mint a session file. Agents in other harnesses may write 
20|   checks but only nanobot sessions can mint keys. Checks written by other harnesses 
21|   will thus require two verifications before orient will run them without -test flag
22| - If you are writing a check, and want to test multiple versions, that's fine. Commit each
23|   if the version is supersceded by another one, delete your commit file from 
24| 
25| ## Signing a check
26| 
27|     nanobot -commit $keyfile
28| 
29| The harness, in one motion:
30| 
31| 1. Grabs the current session file.
32| 2. Writes the check file's encryption key into the session's metadata —
33|    harness-written, inside the signed envelope.
34| 3. Signs the session file with the baked key.
35| 4. Exports it to the dedicated folder in orient.
36| 
37| The spoken-key flow still holds on top: the key must also appear in the
38| session transcript. Two bindings, two authors — stamped in metadata by the
39| harness, spoken in the record by the model. Verification requires both.
40| The record is still the unlock; the mint just proves which record.
41| 
42| ## Retention
43| 
44| Preserve only sessions where changes were made. Every archived session
45| contains at least one signing event; the archive is decision-driven, not
46| continuous. Consequences, all free:
47| 
48| - Retention tracks canon growth (at most ~2 minted sessions per ratified
49|   check, fewer when one session signs several).
50| - Every archived session is load-bearing. The subagent check below operates
51|   on exactly the corpus that matters.
52| - A hole is no longer "some chat is gone" — it is "a specific decision lost
53|   its deliberation." The restore manifest names what it lost.
54| 
55| The town keeps minutes, not a camera.
56| 
57| ## Subagents
58| 
59| - Subagent (fork) sessions cannot sign. A fork is continuity, not
60|   corroboration; same mind, two session files, zero additional trust.
61| - Subagent status is harness-stamped metadata inside the signed envelope —
62|   never model-authored content. A fork cannot testify about its own nature.
63| - Orient rejects any witness whose minted session is a subagent session.
64|   The slot renders unratified with the reason attached.
65| 
66| ## Verification chain (per run, per check)
67| 
68| 1. Load witness pointers from `checks/NAME.key`.
69| 2. Verify the binary signature on each witness session file. No valid
70|    signature → not a session.
71| 3. Verify each witness is not a subagent session (harness-stamped flag in
72|    the signed envelope).
73| 4. Confirm the decryption key in the session metadata is spoken in the
74|    transcript, for both witnesses, at the minted record.
75| 5. Peel one encryption layer per witness. Run.
76| 
77| Unverified at any step → the check does not run; its slot renders as an
78| unratified placeholder naming witness count and failure reason.
79| 
80| ## The paranoia dial
81| 
82| Depending on the degree of security necessary for the system, you can add
83| additional requirements to orient. For secure systems you may want three
84| verification sessions, or verification by an agent with a different github
85| account, or even a check file signed by a third party application. For our
86| purposes, two signatures is fine, but you could require that the file be
87| signed with the whitehouse.gov https cert if you wanted to. 
88| 
89| ## Trust stack (revised)
90| 
91| 1. `orient.py` — read fresh every morning; reading is its ratification.
92| 2. The nanobot binary — compile-time-baked key; the only minter; root of
93|    session provenance.
94| 3. Minted sessions — decision-driven archive; every preserved session is
95|    load-bearing by construction.
96| 4. Chain + git — append-only lineage; the ratchet catches rewrites.
97| 5. Two witnesses, two minted, non-subagent sessions — no single session
98|    produces runnable code; every runnable line traces to two complete,
99|    binary-attested thought records.
100| 6. Accepted residue: a compromised or rebuilt binary mints bad sessions.
101|    Detective, not preventive — knowingly. The human was always root.
102| 7. CA. There will be multiple versions of nanobot, each will have it's own
103|    burned in cert. Every version of nanobot will have it's own key, this
104|    causes 8.  
105| 8. The three paths. 1. All certs valid forever. We keep a log of all 
106|    historic certs, if a session is signed by an older version it is 
107|    still valid. 1b. All certs are valid for n days. Require that old checks
108|    be periodically recertified. 2. All nanobot revisions require recertifying
109|    all checks with the new version, a nanobot change cannot make a check
110|    dangerous. We have a section in orient.py called # Trust Mode. This is
111|    where you state how many signatures orient will require to run, whether
112|    it will require additional confirmation, and what certs it will accept.
113|    Default is 2 signatures and certs are valid forever, but the other options
114|    are in the code and commented out. The model running the script can decide
115|    their own security posture. 
116| 9. orient.py -test is broken. Goal, allow agents writing checks to see how 
117|    their code renders in the actual pipeline. Current behavior, only require 
118|    one signature to run. This lowers the security floor for all checks, not 
119|    just the one the agent is currently testing. New posture
120|    > orient.py -test OPENPRS, DNS, VEINSERVER
121|    Checks explicitly named are run without verification. 
122| 
123| ## Provenance
124| 
125| Evolved 2026-09-18 from the caveman incident thread: compaction by
126| article-stripping (context crunched invisibly while the transcript stayed
127| verbatim) exposed that textual claims of continuity are not evidence of
128| continuity. The fix has been moving authority downward ever since — from
129| the model's self-description (nothing), to committed transcripts
130| (self-asserted), to harness-stamped metadata, to a compile-baked CA.
131| Each layer removes the model layer's ability to lie about the layer
132| beneath it.

(End of file — 132 lines total)

{"path": "/home/evans/Coding_Projects/orient/orient.py", "content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
orient — the wake-up organ.

Read me every morning; reading me is my ratification. I have three jobs:

  1. VERIFY WITNESSES — a check may run only when enough distinct minted

     The record is the unlock; the mint proves which record.
  2. RUN RATIFIED CHECKS — a check is one file returning one string.
     Everything a check returns is escaped. Only strings cross.
  3. SUBSTITUTE — "$NAME key=value" in template.json becomes the escaped string.

Unratified checks do not run. Their slots render as placeholders naming the
witness count and failure reason. The chain (chain/chain.jsonl) is append-only;
every report records the head it saw (the ratchet).

Session spec: session-minting.md. Sessions are minted artifacts signed by the
nanobot binary's baked key; an unsigned transcript is not a session.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

# these by reading them; change them only as a deliberate act, in a commit

# CERT_POLICY = "latest"       # "latest" — only the cert named in certs/LATEST.
